pr_title: systemd: Support OOMPolicy in scope units
pr_comments: (and I'd be fine if the login session scopes are switched over to use OOMPolicy=continue, if you want to add a second commit to this PR. Just add another sd_bus_message() line to manager_start_scope() in src/login/logind-dbus.c)

> I'd be fine if the login session scopes are switched over to use OOMPolicy=continue

Cool. I'll add it. This is definitely the right thing to do--I could imagine scenarios where someone might want the rest of a scope terminated if one process in it gets OOM killed, but definitely not for their login sessions!

Also, if you can give me a hint for what needs to be done in order to make `systemd-run --scope -p OOMPolicy=foo` work, it probably makes sense to do it as part of this PR.
I made the requested changes. Now all `OOMPolicy` modes work as expected (continue, stop, kill), and the policy can also be selected for a transient scope or service when using `systemd-run`.

on every reload. Also the docs haven't been updated. I'll submit a follow-up.

issue_context.title: systemd built-in OOM killer (*not* systemd-oomd) kills all processes in user session/scope unit upon kernel OOM and doesn't respect OOMPolicy=
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

252.1-1-arch

### Used distribution

Arch Linux

### Linux kernel version used

6.0.7-arch1-1

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

x86_64

### Component

systemd

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

Normal kernel OOM killer behavior, because the kernel is able to do the job perfectly well on its own.

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

systemd will kill an entire user slice's scope unit when a process under the scope is OOM killed by the kernel, wrecking *everything* the user was doing instead of limiting the damage to a single offending process. (As a bonus, explicitly disabling this "feature" also doesn't work.)

systemd also lies to you that this will work, even with the reproduction steps below:

```
arch-vm[788]:~% systemctl --user -p DefaultOOMPolicy show
DefaultOOMPolicy=continue
```


### Steps to reproduce the problem

1) Add the following to `/etc/systemd/user.conf.d/resources.conf`:

```
[Manager]
DefaultOOMPolicy=continue
```

Alternatively, edit `/etc/systemd/user.conf` and stick `DefaultOOMPolicy=continue` there; it means the same thing.

2) Run something that eventually triggers the **kernel** OOM killer (this report has **nothing to do with** `systemd-oomd`):

```sh
#!/usr/bin/env sh

exec tail /dev/zero
```

3) After a few seconds, watch as everything you were doing disappears!

### More stuff that doesn't work

* In `/etc/systemd/system.conf`:

  ```
  [Manager]
  DefaultOOMPolicy=continue
  ```

  This will theoretically disable the idiocy for stuff under the system slice, but has no effect on the user slice.

* In `/etc/systemd/system/user-.slice.d/resources.conf` (a "drop-in" which will affect all user slice):

  ```
  [Slice]
  OOMPolicy=continue
  ```

  The `OOMPolicy` key is not recognized under `[Slice]`, while `[Scope]` and `[Service]` are completely unrecognized:

  ```
  Nov 14 15:25:27 arch-vm systemd[1]: /etc/systemd/system/user-.slice.d/resources.conf:2: Unknown key name 'OOMPolicy' in section 'Slice', ignoring.
  ```

* In `/etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d/resources.conf`:
  ```
  [Service]
  OOMPolicy=continue
  ```

  Does nothing.

* In `/etc/systemd/system/session-.scope.d/resources.conf`:

  ```
  [Scope]
  OOMPolicy=continue
  ```

  The `OOMPolicy` key is not recognized under `[Scope]`:

  ```
  Nov 14 15:22:04 arch-vm systemd[1]: /etc/systemd/system/session-.scope.d/resources.conf:2: Unknown key name 'OOMPolicy' in section 'Scope', ignoring.
  ```

### Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue

```sh
Nov 14 11:53:50 arch-vm sshd[8404]: Accepted publickey for mdl from 192.168.204.1 port 54143 ssh2: RSA SHA256:LLfd0TPd0DL8Abh1c/g+Jb8nTV8i1D6BPGM/7VU6wRo
Nov 14 11:53:50 arch-vm sshd[8404]: pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user mdl(uid=1000) by (uid=0)
Nov 14 11:53:50 arch-vm systemd-logind[396]: New session 3 of user mdl.
Nov 14 11:53:50 arch-vm systemd[1]: Started Session 3 of User mdl.
...
Nov 14 12:34:17 arch-vm kernel: oom-kill:constraint=CONSTRAINT_NONE,nodemask=(null),cpuset=/,mems_allowed=0,global_oom,task_memcg=/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-3.scope,task=tail,pid=8656,uid=1000
Nov 14 12:34:17 arch-vm kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 8656 (tail) total-vm:25725656kB, anon-rss:25720108kB, file-rss:4kB, shmem-rss:0kB, UID:1000 pgtables:50388kB oom_score_adj:0
Nov 14 12:34:17 arch-vm systemd[1]: session-3.scope: A process of this unit has been killed by the OOM killer.
Nov 14 12:34:17 arch-vm systemd[1]: session-3.scope: Killing process 8404 (sshd) with signal SIGKILL.
Nov 14 12:34:17 arch-vm systemd[1]: session-3.scope: Killing process 8409 (sshd) with signal SIGKILL.
Nov 14 12:34:17 arch-vm systemd[1]: session-3.scope: Killing process 8411 (zsh) with signal SIGKILL.
Nov 14 12:34:17 arch-vm systemd[1]: session-3.scope: Killing process 8656 (tail) with signal SIGKILL.
Nov 14 12:34:17 arch-vm systemd-logind[396]: Session 3 logged out. Waiting for processes to exit.
Nov 14 12:34:18 arch-vm systemd[1]: session-3.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'.
Nov 14 12:34:18 arch-vm systemd[1]: session-3.scope: Consumed 16.369s CPU time.
Nov 14 12:34:18 arch-vm systemd-logind[396]: Removed session 3.
```
comments:
@yuwata The oomd tag is incorrect. As I explicitly said, **oomd is not enabled** here; this is BUILT-IN systemd behavior. This is shown in the log above:

```
Nov 14 12:34:17 arch-vm systemd[1]: session-3.scope: A process of this unit has been killed by the OOM killer.
```

which corresponds to [this source](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/bf1886226724b3db0779d643195d428575cff0be/src/core/cgroup.c#L3152-L3155).

I can't parse this. "entire user slice's scope"? 

Each user has a slice unit, and each session within it is encapsulated in a scope unit. Hence not sure what an "entire user slice's scope" is supposed to mean?

btw, just to say this clearly: tone it down. "insane" is not appropriate here.

It appears all you are asking for is OOMPolicy= supported in .scope units too?
Yes.

Great. It wasn't obvious if any dbus junk needed to be added, and also systemd itself does some things inconsistently: for example, `src/core/service.c` checks `s->cgroup_context.delegate` directly in `service_add_extras`, while `src/core/scope.c` uses `unit_cgroup_delegate` in `scope_start` (which checks the vtable for `can_delegate` and whatnot) to do presumably the same thing, even though only scope units are passed to `scope_start`, but I don't think any of this matters. Feel free to add your genius to the PR I've just sent; it fixes the problem for me.

To be clear: the patch fixes the problem when `DefaultOOMPolicy=continue` is set as outlined in step 1. (This should be the default, but I'm uninterested in having that fight, having already spent enough time on this.)

~~The patch also does not add support for `systemd-run --scope -p OOMPolicy=whatever`, because I doubt anyone who doesn't want this behavior from systemd would want to selectively change it for specific scopes either when they can already presumably use `OOMScoreAdjust`.~~ (edit: the patch now makes it possible to specify `-p OOMPolicy=whatever` to `systemd-run`)

Are there any known workarounds? I'm affected by this, and it's incredibly annoying...

Nothing like restarting your editor,  all your browser profiles, and a large number of terminal sessions (with their histories lost to the sands of KILL -9) once an hour to really spice up a workday :/
@drvink btw, I'd be fine with switching to OOMPolicy=continue for the scope units created for login sessions. but scopes in generall should probably stick to OOMPolicy=kill
and also, just stop the bs about "junk", "genius", "insane" and stuff. Not the place here for this tone.

> Are there any known workarounds? I'm affected by this, and it's incredibly annoying...

@ralokt Assuming you log in at a tty like a Real Computer Man and not some xdm-using quiche eater, the following steps should protect even your X server from systemd's wrath:

1. `systemd-run --user -p OOMPolicy=continue --service-type=forking -- screen -d -m`
2. `screen -dr`
3. `startx`
4. ???
5. Profit

(I'm pretty sure the issue only affects scope units, so the idea here is simply to run a *service* unit with a process that happens to be something useful for running more stuff.)

@drvink sadly, I really enjoy pastries. However, I guess it might be time for me to complete my coming-of-age ritual :)

Thanks for the suggestion!

Could somebody please post a clear explanation on how to get the fix for this and how to use it?

Should we wait for another systemd release, or was this already released? Would it be systemd v253 as the milestone implies? If yes, when should I expect the release? Which version do I need to have this fixed? Once I have the version, which settings do I need to stop systemd from killing my entire session when a single process goes OOM? Are there any workarounds to use before that?

I'm getting tired of all my precious tmux sessions getting wiped when chrome or firefox get too eager with their memory use :see_no_evil: 

Thank you!
@spbnick ping you distro, they might consider backporting this. But it's really up to them.
@spbnick Try what I posted earlier? I didn't test it but I think it ought to work based on what I understood while diagnosing and fixing the bug.

Thanks, Lennart. Yeah I would go to the distro (Debian) with a question about a backport, if the fixed systemd is not released soon. Or just rebuild it myself with the patch. However, I'd still like to know when the fixed systemd is gonna be released approximately, to perhaps avoid doing the work. And afterwards, I would still like to know how to actually enable the fix.

@drvink, thank you. Do you mean the [comment](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/25376#issuecomment-1326440102) recommending using startx after manual session setup?
@spbnick yes

I found a workaround that doesn't require compiling systemd from source: disable MemoryAccounting for the unit in question (or DefaultMemoryAccounting=no in user.conf). The oom-kill status stuff is disabled in systemd if memory accounting is off, even for scope units before OOMPolicy was implemented for it.
I just installed ElasticSearch on manjaro, the oom-killer killed it for whatever reason and systemd decided to SIGKILL everything in `session-2.scope`, destroying my X session.

It's incredible that systemd is doing some oom killing after kernel already did his job even if I have no systemd-oomd installed.

I'm constantly loosing my entire X session because of Teams (even on 16GB PC) which is properly killed by Kernel and it should be enough. Why is then system killing entire user session implemented for???!!!  We have pretty nice Deny of Service by single memory leaking process!

Why I have to reconfigure all PCs that I'm responsible for because you decided to activate this KILL EVERYTHING "feature" by default? Thanks to that "feature" Linux looks very professional...

Yet another problem created by systemd replacing piece by piece every part of Linux with it's mysterious behaviors. Now it's time to replace kernel features. Nice....

So just to confirm, the global workaround here is set `DefaultOOMPolicy=continue` in `/etc/system/system.conf`? That means if a process in a unit is killed the rest of the unit keeps continues running?

> So just to confirm, the global workaround here is set `DefaultOOMPolicy=continue` in `/etc/system/system.conf`? That means if a process in a unit is killed the rest of the unit keeps continues running?

* Short answer: probably, but may depend on distro. See `systemd-system.conf(5)` for pathname details.
* Long answer: for me on on Ubuntu 22.04.3 LTS jammy -- rather than risk changing the distro-managed `/etc/system/systemd.conf` -- I chose to add the line to new file `/etc/systemd/system.conf.d/local.conf` instead
Just adding my 2 cents on this one. The poor OOM documentation needs to be addressed.

review_comments: If the policy is OOM_STOP, then the unit will be terminated, just like before. (As I said in the issue thread, I don't think this is a good default or even a useful behavior, but unless you want to change it, this edit does not change the old behavior, so the code is fine.)
well, what I am saying is that if OOM_STOP is set we should not enter SCOPE_STOP_SIGKILL right-away as the code will do now, but SCOPE_STOP_SIGTERM instead.
